procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants appealed to the Patna High Court. The High Court judge reviewed the evidence and concluded that the consignment found in the wagon at 2 p.m. on May 15, 1960, was the same consignment loaded by the appellants at Sheonarayanpur on the afternoon of May 13, 1960. The High Court seemingly upheld the conviction or some aspect of the lower court's decision, as the appellants then sought special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants sought and were granted special leave to appeal the Patna High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court heard the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 240 of 1966).

issue.issue_text: Whether the false representation made by the appellants in obtaining a railway receipt, by misdescribing the goods consigned, cast any additional liability or risk on the railway, thereby causing damage or harm sufficient to constitute the offence of cheating.

facts: The appellants obtained a railway receipt by falsely representing that a consignment contained 251 bags of chillies, when it actually contained 197 bags of straw.
The Station Master, acting on this representation, issued the receipt.

The railway receipt included notations that the consignment was "said to be" 251 bags of chillies and that the weight was based on "senders' weight accepted" (S.W.A.), indicating the railway had not verified the contents or weight.
law: The offence of cheating requires that an act or omission, induced by deception, causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to the person deceived.

Under the Indian Railways Act and the Goods Tariff General Rules, a railway receipt does not constitute an admission by the railway that the description or weight of the goods as furnished by the consignor is correct.
In case of a claim for loss or damage, the burden of proof is on the owner to prove the actual contents, weight, and value of the goods they put on the train.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the railway did not run any additional risk or incur any additional liability due to the false description on the receipt.
The disclaimers on the receipt (such as "said to be" and "S.W.A.") protected the railway, as it had not accepted the consignment as being chillies or admitted to its weight.

If the goods were lost or damaged, the railway's liability would not be based on the false description. Instead, the appellants would have to prove that they had actually loaded 251 bags of chillies to make a successful claim.
Since the railway's potential liability was not increased by the misrepresentation, the act of issuing the receipt was not likely to cause any damage or harm to the railway.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the false representation did not cast any additional liability or risk on the railway, and therefore was not likely to cause it any damage or harm, a necessary element of the offence of cheating was absent. Consequently, the appellants were not guilty of cheating the railway.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the false representation made by the appellants in obtaining a railway receipt, by misdescribing the goods consigned, cast any additional liability or risk on the railway, thereby causing damage or harm sufficient to constitute the offence of cheating.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued they were not guilty of cheating because the Station Master did not act upon their declaration as being correct.
This was evidenced by the Station Master writing on the railway receipt that the consignment was 'said to be 251 bags of dry chillies', which showed he was not fully deceived.
respondent_arguments: The appellants made a false representation, both orally and in the forwarding note, that the goods were chillies when they were actually straw.
On the strength of this false representation, the appellants induced the Station Master to issue a valuable security, the railway receipt, for 251 bags of dry chillies.
The Station Master's endorsement 'S.W.A.' (senders' weight accepted) also demonstrated that he was acting upon the declaration made by the appellants.

cases.case_name: Dominion of India v. Firm Museram Kishunprasad
cases.principle: A railway receipt that qualifies the number of items with the remark 'said to contain' does not act as an admission by the railway of the correctness of the quantity stated; the number is mentioned merely to calculate the freight.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. S, p, Lekhu Reddiar
cases.principle: The case was approved alongside Dominion of India v. Firm Museram Kishunprasad, supporting the principle regarding the qualified evidentiary value of a railway receipt marked 'said to contain'.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A false representation made to obtain a railway receipt does not constitute the offense of cheating if the receipt does not cast any additional liability on the railway and is therefore not likely to cause any damage or harm to it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the false representation made by the appellants in obtaining the railway receipt, by misdescribing the goods, did not constitute the offence of cheating. This was because the act did not cast any additional liability on the railway, and therefore, the issuance of the receipt was not likely to cause any damage or harm to the railway or the Station Master. Since the element of causing or being likely to cause damage or harm was not met, a necessary component of the offence of cheating was absent.
legal_tests_applied: To constitute cheating, the act or omission induced by deception must cause or be 'likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property.'
